items.stem: McDonald's menus in India do not include beef because:
options: beef is not available anywhere in Asia
it is too expensive to import
India banned all fast food
most Hindus do not eat beef
items.answer: most Hindus do not eat beef
items.markingKey: D. The Maharaja Mac uses chicken.

items.stem: "Cultural diffusion only happens through TNCs." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Migration, tourism, education, religion and social media are also major channels.
items.markingKey: Migration, tourism, education, religion and social media are also major channels. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between glocalisation and cultural imperialism.
items.answer: Cultural imperialism is the imposition of a dominant culture on others; glocalisation is the adaptation of global products to fit local culture.
items.markingKey: Cultural imperialism is the imposition of a dominant culture on others; glocalisation is the adaptation of global products to fit local culture. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A fieldwork survey recorded the reasons given by 40 shoppers in Hanoi for choosing a local market over a supermarket: price 6, freshness 19, supporting local producers 12, convenience 3. Test the null hypothesis that there is no preference between categories using the chi-squared test (χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E; critical value at 0.05 for 3 degrees of freedom = 7.81).
items.answer: E = 10 per category; χ² = 15.00; df = 3; significant - reject the null hypothesis
items.markingKey: M1 expected 40/4 = 10; M1 Σ(O − E)²/E; A1 χ² = 15.00; A1 df = 3; R1 compare with 7.81: reject H₀.

items.stem: Between 1995 and 2015 the inward FDI stock of a Central European EU member changed from 93.1 to 176.3 US$ billion. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (176.3 − 93.1) ÷ 93.1 × 100; A1 +89.4% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

(a) Calculate the percentage of fast-food customers who preferred local adapted items. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, explain what the survey suggests about glocalisation. [6]
items.answer: (a) 41/64 × 100 = 64.1% (b) Most customers of global chains preferred adapted local items, suggesting glocalisation helps global brands succeed.
items.markingKey: (a) 41/64 × 100 = 64.1% (b) Most customers of global chains preferred adapted local items, suggesting glocalisation helps global brands succeed. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The imposition of one culture, often Western or American, over others through media, brands and economic power"?
options: diaspora
Americanisation
cultural imperialism
ethnic enclave
items.answer: cultural imperialism
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of cultural imperialism.

items.stem: Explain how the media contribute to cultural diffusion.
items.answer: Films, TV, streaming platforms (Netflix), social media and music spread values, language, fashion and consumer brands worldwide almost instantly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Films, TV, streaming platforms (Netflix), social media and music spread values, language, fashion and consumer brands worldwide almost instantly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why some people see globalisation as cultural imperialism.
items.answer: Dominant Western media, brands and English language spread through economic power, can displace local languages, foods and traditions, and promote consumerism.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Dominant Western media, brands and English language spread through economic power, can displace local languages, foods and traditions, and promote consumerism. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between cultural homogenisation and cultural hybridity.
items.answer: Homogenisation reduces diversity as places become more similar; hybridity creates new cultural forms by mixing elements from different cultures.
items.markingKey: Homogenisation reduces diversity as places become more similar; hybridity creates new cultural forms by mixing elements from different cultures. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe the Korean Wave and explain what it reveals about multi-directional cultural flows.
items.answer: K-pop and Korean dramas reached audiences across Asia, the Americas and Europe, and Squid Game became Netflix's most-watched series in 2021. Non-Western culture can spread globally through digital platforms.
items.markingKey: Context (K-pop and Korean dramas reached audiences across Asia, the Americas and Europe, and Squid Game became Netflix's most-watched series in 2021.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Non-Western culture can spread globally through digital platforms. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to multi-directional cultural flows.

items.stem: A fieldwork survey recorded the identity chosen by 39 second-generation migrants surveyed in Sydney: host nationality only 10, heritage nationality only 21, dual (hyphenated) identity 8. Test the null hypothesis that there is no preference between categories using the chi-squared test (χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E; critical value at 0.05 for 2 degrees of freedom = 5.99).
items.answer: E = 13 per category; χ² = 7.54; df = 2; significant - reject the null hypothesis
items.markingKey: M1 expected 39/3 = 13; M1 Σ(O − E)²/E; A1 χ² = 7.54; A1 df = 2; R1 compare with 5.99: reject H₀.

items.stem: "Globalisation is leading to cultural homogenisation." To what extent do you agree with this statement? In your answer, consider the perspectives of different stakeholders.
items.answer: Global culture spreads, but it is adapted, resisted and mixed rather than simply homogenised.
items.markingKey: Paper 3 (b) indicative content - for: spread of global brands, English and Hollywood; loss of languages and traditions. Against: glocalisation and hybridity; reverse flows (K-pop, Nollywood) and revival of local identities. Judgement: Global culture spreads, but it is adapted, resisted and mixed rather than simply homogenised. items.stem: The world's largest diaspora by country of origin is that of:
items.answer: India (about 18 million emigrants)

items.stem: Explain why second-generation migrants often develop hybrid identities.
items.answer: They grow up between their parents' heritage culture at home and the host culture at school and work, combining language, faith, food and values to create new identities such as "British Asian".

items.stem: Explain the difference between an ethnic enclave and a diaspora.
items.answer: A diaspora is a dispersed global population sharing an origin; an ethnic enclave is a specific neighbourhood with a concentration of one group.
items.markingKey: A diaspora is a dispersed global population sharing an origin; an ethnic enclave is a specific neighbourhood with a concentration of one group. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Lebanon received about US$5.9 billion in personal remittances in a year when its GDP was about US$20 billion. Calculate remittances as a percentage of GDP. items.stem: Explain how diasporas spread culture.
items.answer: Migrants bring food, music, religion, festivals and language to host societies (e.g. Diwali in Leicester, Notting Hill Carnival); they also send ideas and goods home, and online media connect diaspora and homeland.

items.stem: Examine the view that diasporas are the most important way in which culture spreads.
items.answer: Diasporas are a powerful channel, especially for everyday culture, but media and TNCs spread culture more widely.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: bring food, faith and music directly into host societies; transnational links. Against / limitations: media, TNCs and the internet reach far more people; tourism and education also spread culture. A supported conclusion might be: Diasporas are a powerful channel, especially for everyday culture, but media and TNCs spread culture more widely. items.stem: Explain how cultural diffusion, cultural imperialism and glocalisation are changing cultures.
items.answer: Indicative content: Channels of diffusion (media, TNCs, migration, internet); Americanisation; glocalisation (McDonald's, Netflix); reverse flows (K-pop, Nollywood); resistance (France).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An area of a city with a concentration of one ethnic or cultural group, e.g. Chinatown in San Francisco"?
options: language revitalisation
ethnic enclave
language endangerment
Greenberg's diversity index
items.answer: ethnic enclave
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of ethnic enclave.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "cultural homogenisation".
items.answer: The reduction of cultural diversity as a dominant global culture spreads
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the reduction of cultural diversity as a dominant global culture spreads. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: UNESCO estimates that what proportion of the world's languages are endangered?
items.answer: About 40%
items.markingKey: About 40%. Many have fewer than 1,000 speakers.

items.stem: Distinguish between a diaspora and an ethnic enclave.
items.answer: A diaspora is a dispersed global population sharing an origin; an ethnic enclave is a specific neighbourhood with a concentration of one group.
items.markingKey: A diaspora is a dispersed global population sharing an origin; an ethnic enclave is a specific neighbourhood with a concentration of one group. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why global brands often adopt glocalisation strategies.
items.answer: Local tastes, religions, languages and laws vary; adapting products (McDonald's McAloo Tikki, KFC's congee in China) increases sales and acceptance and reduces opposition to foreign firms.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Local tastes, religions, languages and laws vary; adapting products (McDonald's McAloo Tikki, KFC's congee in China) increases sales and acceptance and reduces opposition to foreign firms. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the loss of languages matters.
items.answer: Languages carry knowledge of local environments, medicine, history and identity; their loss reduces cultural diversity and can harm wellbeing of indigenous communities.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Languages carry knowledge of local environments, medicine, history and identity; their loss reduces cultural diversity and can harm wellbeing of indigenous communities. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between multiculturalism and assimilation.
items.answer: Assimilation expects migrants to adopt the host culture and lose distinctive traits; multiculturalism supports groups keeping their identities within shared laws and citizenship.
items.markingKey: Assimilation expects migrants to adopt the host culture and lose distinctive traits; multiculturalism supports groups keeping their identities within shared laws and citizenship. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Globalisation is making all cultures identical." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Global flows also strengthen local identities, create hybrid forms and spread non-Western culture.
items.markingKey: Global flows also strengthen local identities, create hybrid forms and spread non-Western culture. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between religious diversity and linguistic diversity.
items.answer: Linguistic diversity is the variety of languages spoken in an area; religious diversity is the variety of faiths practised.
items.markingKey: Linguistic diversity is the variety of languages spoken in an area; religious diversity is the variety of faiths practised. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A fieldwork survey recorded the music that 80 secondary students surveyed in Mexico City stream most: local artists 17, US/UK artists 59, K-pop 1, Latin artists 3. Test the null hypothesis that there is no preference between categories using the chi-squared test (χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E; critical value at 0.05 for 3 degrees of freedom = 7.81).
items.answer: E = 20 per category; χ² = 109.00; df = 3; significant - reject the null hypothesis
items.markingKey: M1 expected 80/4 = 20; M1 Σ(O − E)²/E; A1 χ² = 109.00; A1 df = 3; R1 compare with 7.81: reject H₀.

items.stem: A fieldwork survey recorded the views of 48 residents interviewed about a new foreign-owned factory in Tangier: support 20, neutral 19, oppose 9. Test the null hypothesis that there is no preference between categories using the chi-squared test (χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E; critical value at 0.05 for 2 degrees of freedom = 5.99).
items.answer: E = 16 per category; χ² = 4.62; df = 2; not significant - accept the null hypothesis
items.markingKey: M1 expected 48/3 = 16; M1 Σ(O − E)²/E; A1 χ² = 4.62; A1 df = 2; R1 compare with 5.99: accept H₀.

items.stem: A fieldwork survey recorded the language used on 39 shop signs recorded along a main street in Bangkok: local language only 1, English only 11, bilingual 27. Test the null hypothesis that there is no preference between categories using the chi-squared test (χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E; critical value at 0.05 for 2 degrees of freedom = 5.99).
items.answer: E = 13 per category; χ² = 26.46; df = 2; significant - reject the null hypothesis
items.markingKey: M1 expected 39/3 = 13; M1 Σ(O − E)²/E; A1 χ² = 26.46; A1 df = 2; R1 compare with 5.99: reject H₀.

items.stem: Briefly describe Chinatown in San Francisco and explain what it reveals about ethnic enclaves.
items.answer: Founded in the 1840s, it is the oldest Chinatown in North America. Concentrations of migrants preserve and display cultural identity.
items.markingKey: Context (Founded in the 1840s, it is the oldest Chinatown in North America.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Concentrations of migrants preserve and display cultural identity. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to ethnic enclaves.

items.stem: A fieldwork survey recorded the music that 48 secondary students surveyed in Istanbul stream most: local artists 17, US/UK artists 14, K-pop 5, Latin artists 12. Test the null hypothesis that there is no preference between categories using the chi-squared test (χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E; critical value at 0.05 for 3 degrees of freedom = 7.81).
items.answer: E = 12 per category; χ² = 6.50; df = 3; not significant - accept the null hypothesis
items.markingKey: M1 expected 48/4 = 12; M1 Σ(O − E)²/E; A1 χ² = 6.50; A1 df = 3; R1 compare with 7.81: accept H₀.

items.stem: Using a named example, explain how a minority language has been revitalised.
items.answer: e.g. Welsh: the Welsh Language Act 1993 and 2011 Measure, Welsh-medium schools, S4C TV channel (1982) and bilingual signs; about 538,000 speakers (17.8%) in 2021, with the goal of a million by 2050.
items.markingKey: e.g. Welsh: the Welsh Language Act 1993 and 2011 Measure, Welsh-medium schools, S4C TV channel (1982) and bilingual signs; about 538,000 speakers (17.8%) in 2021, with the goal of a million by 2050.

items.stem: Using the Filipino diaspora as an example, explain transnational ties.
items.answer: About 10 million Filipinos live or work abroad, sending remittances equal to about 9% of GDP. Migrants maintain strong economic and family links with home.
items.markingKey: Context (About 10 million Filipinos live or work abroad, sending remittances equal to about 9% of GDP.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Migrants maintain strong economic and family links with home. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to transnational ties.

items.stem: Outline one argument for and one argument against the view that globalisation is leading to cultural homogenisation.
items.answer: Global culture spreads, but it is adapted, resisted and mixed rather than simply homogenised.
items.markingKey: For: spread of global brands, English and Hollywood. Against: glocalisation and hybridity. [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the Greenberg diversity index is a useful measure of cultural diversity?
items.answer: It is useful for comparing linguistic diversity, but it captures only one aspect of culture.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: simple, comparable, probability-based; easy to calculate from census data. Against / limitations: ignores multilingualism, dialects and other cultural traits; depends on census categories. A supported conclusion might be: It is useful for comparing linguistic diversity, but it captures only one aspect of culture.
